episode_thesis: Andrew Beer argues that 60/40 was a historical accident of a 20-year bond bull market, that every equity crisis broke the previous diversifier playbook while the SG CTA index (low correlation, crisis alpha, controlled index drawdowns, a net Sharpe of 0.34) held up, and that managed futures will only go mainstream by being reframed in allocators' language as incremental, tactical diversification and relabelled 'contrarian tactical alpha'. Niels Kaastrup-Larsen adds the complex-adaptive-systems rationale for trend following, current performance numbers and the view that allocators time the space badly and are held back by due-diligence fixation on details.

worldview_premises.premise: 60/40 was a historical accident of the 2000s: a 20-year bond bull market and a short window of negative stock-bond correlation made bonds the perfect diversifier; extrapolating it forward is a mistake, and benchmarking everyone to it produced herding and now an existential crisis.
worldview_premises.support: Stock-bond correlation history and the 27-year SG CTA data set; end-2021 allocators added bonds at the peak.

worldview_premises.premise: Capital markets assumptions are 10-year predictions of 25-40 assets and their correlations extrapolated from recent decades, anchored on a cash return most people got wrong; they are always wrong.
worldview_premises.support: Personal observation of asset allocation since the early 2000s; the late-1990s commodity series with negative correlation that later flipped positive.

worldview_premises.premise: Asset allocation rests on diversification (free lunch) and not trading tactically because humans time markets badly, so a whole-portfolio view prevents behavioural losses; yet 10-year predictability over 3-month unpredictability is a bit crazy and the rationale is discipline.
worldview_premises.support: Morningstar investor-return studies; dot-com and GFC blow-ups.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors hold bonds for the regular coupon, an emotional rather than real-return reason; the stock-bond breakdown pushes them to replace some or all of the 40 with alternatives.
worldview_premises.support: Anecdote of a client asking why he owns bonds.

worldview_premises.premise: Each equity crisis broke the previous diversifier playbook (2000-02: bonds +30%, REITs +49%; GFC: high yield -22%, REITs and commodities failed; 2022: bonds -15-20%, REITs -25%, gold flat) while the SG CTA index gained each time, so crisis alpha (judged only against equity bear markets) is the strongest argument for the space.
worldview_premises.support: SG CTA index (20 largest managed futures funds since January 2000) versus asset classes in three crises.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following structurally profits from big price moves away from consensus (buying what doubles, shorting what halves; "contrarian tactical alpha") and so should do well in a crisis; it is early, not late.
worldview_premises.support: Gold bought at 2100 and ridden to 5500; crude at 60 in January 2026.

worldview_premises.premise: Tactical trading controls drawdowns because managed futures do not white-knuckle hold losers: SG CTA max monthly drawdown 16% versus US Agg 17%, S&P 51%, Nasdaq 81%, REITs 69%, gold 42%, commodities 87%.
worldview_premises.support: 27 years of index data; caveat that single funds are about 25% and index composition changes.

worldview_premises.premise: Low correlation to traditional assets is the strongest input for including CTAs on an efficient frontier, regardless of daily sign; the 2000-2020 negative stock-bond correlation was an anomaly (27-year: US IG +0.36, REITs 0.65, GSCI 0.3, gold about 0, CTAs slightly negative).
worldview_premises.support: Correlation table.

worldview_premises.premise: CTA alpha versus the S&P 500 was about 330 bp a year over 27 years, high among hedge fund strategies, and valuable because of low correlation; bond alpha 50-150 bp, gold 9% mostly from its recent surge; alpha is a measure of hidden equity exposure.
worldview_premises.support: Index regression; his paper on alpha.

worldview_premises.premise: The SG CTA index net Sharpe is 0.34 (about cash plus 275 bp, volatility below 10%) after trading costs and 1.4%/14% fees, comparable to traditional assets (about 0.4) and above commodities; hedge fund and illiquid Sharpes are inflated by selection bias and non-marking; with low correlation and crisis alpha, allocators would hold the product even at zero Sharpe.
worldview_premises.support: Index net-of-fee data; Millennium comparison.

worldview_premises.premise: Returns are lumpy (+13% 2008, nothing 2009-13, +16% 2014, +20% 2022, below cash three years, strong 2026); tolerable for 10-year allocators but hard for quarterly committees and wealth clients.
worldview_premises.support: Annual SG CTA returns.

worldview_premises.premise: Fund dispersion is wide and persistence is absent, so differences are mostly modelling luck; performance-chasing selection fails, and manager claims about model nuances cannot be evaluated by allocators.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of fund returns and allocator conversations.

worldview_premises.premise: Discretionary tactical timers are dangerous: of 20 managers going into the GFC five got it right and built large businesses, 15 blew up.
worldview_premises.support: Recollection of US tactical strategies in the 2000s.

worldview_premises.premise: Concentrating a 5% allocation in the single best manager (AQR's mutual fund reached $14.3bn) and then blaming the whole space for its later 20% drawdown, together with timing the space badly, created the sentiment trough of the late 2010s and early 2020s.
worldview_premises.support: AQR story; allocator conversations.

worldview_premises.premise: AI lowers the capital and headcount needed to start a business, like the dot-com boom in the 1990s which raised entrepreneurial risk tolerance and US growth; AI capex spending is bizarre economics and the equity market has become one large venture-capital play on AI.
worldview_premises.support: 1990s experience; examples of one-person businesses using Claude.

worldview_premises.premise: Growth for CTAs requires a simple story in allocators' language (relabel as contrarian tactical alpha, as LBOs became private equity), because the chain from committees to advisers to clients must be able to explain it and institutions already own the space.
worldview_premises.support: Industry relabelling history; conference experience.

decision_process.practice: Add managed futures at the margin by replacing part of the 40 rather than replacing the framework; frame as the 10% tactical complement to a 90% right SAA.
decision_process.why: Allocators will keep 60/40 but need incremental change.

decision_process.practice: Study the space through the SG CTA index (20 largest funds) to lower idiosyncratic risk and see behaviour across environments.
decision_process.why: The sector is more predictable than any one fund.

decision_process.practice: Hold several funds (diversify across funds) because individual funds have about 25% max drawdowns versus 16% for the index.
Pair two complementary CTA funds and evaluate on a 10-year horizon.
decision_process.why: Guarantees a good story each year; avoids timing.

decision_process.practice: Do not concentrate in a single best manager or chase recent top funds.
Evaluate crisis alpha only against equity bear markets and judge the product on correlation, crisis alpha, alpha, drawdown control, Sharpe and lumpiness.

Frame in the allocator's language: relabel as contrarian tactical alpha, use examples (crude at 60, gold 2100 to 5500, shorts in Treasuries in December 2021), offer ETFs/mutual funds compared with the liquid portfolio rather than hedge fund targets.
decision_process.why: Stories enable committees, advisers and clients.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 16% max drawdown is for an index average of 20 funds that changes over time; individual funds are about 25% and up to the high 40s including departed funds, which weakens the "controlled drawdown" claim; Beer states this himself.
Sharpe 0.34 is after fees, whereas equity and bond Sharpes are free and not investable, so the comparison is asymmetric (stated by Beer). The "rates 46" and "gold 6" figures are garbled in captions.
Crisis alpha is defined as equity bear markets only; three data points (2000-02, GFC, 2022 minor crisis) and the 2022 case is not an equity bear market of 40%, so evidence is sparse.
Beer says tactical timing by humans is dangerous (15 of 20 blew up) yet trend following is itself tactical; the distinction (rules versus discretion) is implied, not argued.
Beer's claim of no persistence in manager returns is asserted without data on air, and he nonetheless recommends pairing two specific complementary funds.
The AI-as-venture-capital-play and bond-tantrum comments are impressionistic, with no indicators or horizon.
Interest incentives: Beer sells a managed futures ETF; Niels openly states a bias for trend following.
Recollection that AQR's fund hit $14.3bn and then fell 20% is from memory.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observable inputs named: bond market tantrum signs (yields rising), oil and commodity structure, AI equity concentration, stock-bond correlation sign, and allocator reaction. Horizons: 10-year allocator horizon for evaluating CTAs; no price targets.
reader_inferences: (reader) Beer's case rests on three conditions: stock-bond correlation positive and persistent, equity crises happening at intervals, and CTAs' low correlation continuing; the 2022 crisis shows the third held.

(reader) His emphasis on narrative implies that flows into CTAs are a function of allocator career incentives, so product adoption may lag evidence and then surge after strong years (2022, 2026), with timing risk for late entrants.
(reader) Pairing two funds and 10-year horizon is Beer's behavioural hedge against manager dispersion; it implicitly accepts that fund selection cannot be improved by analysis.
